domain_label: Turlock Independent Home & Contractor Trades — Business Models & Unit Economics
purpose: A method for reasoning about how each independent home-and-contractor-trade format in Turlock and Stanislaus County is actually run as a business — its trucks-tools-and-license capital base, crew and owner-operator labor model, CSLB/bond/workers-comp licensing gate, cost structure and labeled benchmark margins, shared supply-house chain, and the operating decisions that make each sub-category viable or doom it — without ever stating a named business's dollar revenue as fact.
assumptions: no observed per-business financials supplied; every dollar band is a labeled industry-benchmark estimate (revenue per truck/technician/employee/crew) scaled by an observable size signal (years in business, residential-vs-commercial mix, showroom presence, 24/7 dispatch, fleet language), tagged estimate-not-actual, never a claim of actual revenue for any named business

the universe is the 22 verified independent home-trade firms in Turlock catalogued in businesses.json (chains and big-box installed services excluded), in a town of ~72,900 residents in ~23-25k households at a median household income of ~$82,995, set in a dense Stanislaus dairy/nut/food-processing belt

city, county, state and demographic figures used here (population, income, ancestry shares, CSLB rules, bond and permit fees) are cited public facts from the deep-dive or labeled derivations, not invented

supplier-to-named-business links are representative inference about the realistic supply-house universe (Ferguson, Hajoca, SiteOne, Ewing, Graybar, WAXIE, etc.), not confirmed accounts, unless a cited source states the relationship
cost-structure and margin benchmarks are published trade-contractor figures (gross/labor/material/net) applied as planning priors, not audited operator P&Ls
exclusions: chain, franchise and big-box installed-services trade operations (Home Depot/Lowe's flooring, Roto-Rooter-class brands, regional HVAC chains — the catalog is independents only)
stating any actual dollar revenue, profit, or owner income for a specifically named Turlock business as fact
demand-and-saturation market sizing as a standalone deliverable beyond what is needed to judge a sub-category's viability (the sizing detail lives in the market/reconciled analyses)
general handyman, solo cash-basis informal operators, and the uncataloged tail except where they bear on the coverage-floor caveat
tax, legal, and licensing-filing advice for an individual operator; this models formats and decisions, not a specific CSLB application

competency_questions.acceptance_condition: ENTRY_GO_NOGO composes saturation, the licensing/labor gate and demand headroom into a defensible add/avoid verdict (no ninth commodity-mowing landscaper, no fourth residential cleaner; favor independent electrical, commercial HVAC, premium landscape, and succession acquisition) each conditioned on clearing the CSLB and skilled-labor gate

glossary.definition: The binding honesty label on every dollar band in this KB: the figure is a published trade-contractor benchmark (revenue per truck/technician/employee/crew) scaled by an observable Turlock size signal, never a reported or claimed actual revenue for any named business.

The structural division of the sector into Engine A (licensed, event-driven mechanical trades — electrical, HVAC, plumbing — with CSLB/bond/skilled-labor moats) and Engine B (easy-entry, labor-is-the-product recurring services — janitorial, landscape maintenance — defended only by contract retention).

The CSLB threshold under which any project where labor plus materials totals $500 or more requires a contractor license; covered home-trade work above it cannot be legally bid without the relevant Class-C classification.

An observable proxy (years in business, residential-vs-commercial language, showroom presence, 24/7 dispatch, fleet/crew language) used to scale a published per-truck/per-tech/per-employee benchmark into a planning revenue band, in place of unavailable actual sales.

The reported sector density (22 firms / 73k residents x 10,000 = 3.0 per 10k) is a floor counting only web-present independents; the cash-basis informal tail pushes true operating density to a labeled-estimate 5-8 per 10k.

The demand cap created by Modesto (~218k residents, 15 miles north) hosting larger trade firms, supply houses, franchise players and big-box installed services that siphon high-ticket and specialty jobs, thinning the Turlock-headquartered count.

The binding constraint on the licensed trades: journeyman/apprentice electricians, HVAC techs and plumbers cannot be conjured quickly, so labor is a hard supply limit not just a cost line, and is the main reason the gated trades stay thin.

The branch-wholesaler just-in-time model in which a contractor draws pipe/wire/fittings/condensers/sprinkler heads from a local supply house on a trade-credit account for booked work, holding almost no finished-goods inventory.

The workers-comp rule that any contractor with employees must carry coverage, with C-20 HVAC unable to claim an exemption regardless of employee status; the SB 216 push toward WC-for-all-licensees was deferred from 1/1/2026 to 1/1/2028 by SB 1455.

The caveat that a high-revenue trade band (established multi-truck plumbing/HVAC, flooring) can post strong gross while netting only 5-20%, so revenue must never be read as profit; emergency repair is the highest-margin work, install the thinnest.

nodes.definition: Establish the demand floor every Turlock home-trade format draws on: ~72,900 residents in ~23-25k households at a median household income of ~$82,995, an aging core housing stock (1950s-1990s) driving recurring repair/replacement, a dense light-commercial and ag/food-facility belt that anchors recurring janitorial/HVAC/electrical contracts, and property managers whose apartment turns drive move-out cleaning, flooring and plumbing. Demand splits sharply by discretion — plumbing/HVAC/electrical are non-discretionary and event-driven, janitorial and landscape maintenance are recurring-contract, and flooring and landscape install are rate-sensitive and discretionary. This out-of-pocket, income/rate-sensitive base is the size of the pie before any sub-category question is asked.

included: resident population, income and household count
homeowner, light-commercial and property-manager demand sources
the discretionary vs non-discretionary demand split
aging-housing-stock replacement driver

pros.claim: Sizing the base from cited public figures grounds every sub-category judgment in real local demand instead of national job-board noise
pros.example: the ~23-25k households on aging 1950s-1990s stock set a defensible recurring repair/replacement ceiling

cons.claim: The city figure understates the true addressable base because rural south-Stanislaus trade-area draw is left unquantified
cons.example: reading 73k residents as the whole market ignores the unmeasured rural draw that makes the saturation read conservative

failure_modes: treating the resident base as the independents' addressable revenue without subtracting Modesto leakage and the informal tail
ignoring the rate-sensitivity of out-of-pocket discretionary flooring and install demand
acceptance_tests: the demand base cites population, household count and median income, names the homeowner/light-commercial/property-manager sources, and splits demand into discretionary vs non-discretionary, all labeled estimate where derived
revisit_triggers: a Census ACS refresh changes population or income
interest rates or remodel budgets shift discretionary install demand
a major commercial or ag-facility account base changes

base.update_signal: a population, income, household, or rate-driven demand figure is updated

nodes.definition: Tie the sector's defining structure to the sub-categories each engine sustains. Engine A — licensed, event-driven mechanical trades (electrical, HVAC, plumbing) — carries real moats: a CSLB license tied to a Responsible Managing Officer, bonds, workers' comp, EPA refrigerant certification, and the binding skilled-journeyman-labor constraint; demand is non-discretionary (a dead water heater, a failed AC in July, a tripping panel). Engine B — easy-entry, labor-is-the-product recurring services (janitorial/cleaning, landscape maintenance) — has near-zero licensing barriers, thin supply chains and low capex, selling recurring crew-hours on standing accounts defended only by contract retention. This moat-strength-vs-saturation division — thin licensed trades, crowded easy-entry tail — is the spine of the entire analysis, supported by Turlock's labor-rich Hispanic/Assyrian/Portuguese-Azorean entrepreneurial base.

included: Engine A licensed-trade moats and Engine B easy-entry profile
which sub-categories fall on each engine
the labor-rich community base behind the crowded tail

pros.claim: Splitting the sector into two engines explains both why a sub-category is thin or crowded and where its defensibility lives
pros.example: the two cataloged electrical firms are thin because the same moat that protects them suppresses new entry

cons.claim: The clean two-engine line blurs at cross-sellers that straddle both (plumbing-primary firms carrying HVAC)
cons.example: DeHart and Turlock Plumbing H&A sit in Engine A plumbing while adding HVAC capacity the headline count misses

failure_modes: assuming an Engine-B easy-entry sub-category has the same defensibility as an Engine-A licensed one
missing that functional HVAC capacity (~4) exceeds the headline primary count because of cross-sellers
acceptance_tests: each engine is defined with its moats or lack of them and mapped to the specific sub-categories it sustains, noting the cross-seller straddle
revisit_triggers: a licensing or labor-supply change shifts an Engine-A moat
a new entrant or closure changes an engine's count
a cross-seller adds or drops a secondary trade line

base.update_signal: an engine's moat, count, or cross-seller straddle changes

nodes.definition: Account for the single biggest cap on the Turlock-headquartered trade count: Modesto, roughly triple the population and 15 miles north, hosts the regional concentration of larger trade firms, supply houses, national/franchise players (Roto-Rooter-class plumbing/drain brands, regional HVAC chains) and big-box installed services (Home Depot/Lowe's flooring, water heaters, HVAC). High-ticket and specialty jobs leak north, thinning the local count, with additional leak channels through lead aggregators (Angi/Thumbtack/Yelp) that commoditize price and DIY product purchasing that pulls margin out of flooring and plumbing supply. Any count judgment that ignores this leakage will over-state Turlock headroom — especially for high-ticket, cross-shopped flooring and specialty mechanical work, less so for emergency-dispatch and relationship-driven recurring services.

included: Modesto's size and proximity
which job types and channels leak to it
which sub-categories are most vs least exposed to leakage
excluded: the measured leakage figure (it is an estimate of cross-shop behavior, not a count)

pros.claim: Naming the leakage explains why population alone over-predicts Turlock's trade count
pros.example: high-ticket flooring leaks to big-box and Modesto retailers, so two showrooms sit at ceiling not headroom

cons.claim: The leakage is an estimate of cross-shopping behavior, not a measured figure, so it can be over- or under-applied
cons.example: assuming all specialty work leaks when local emergency dispatch retains a loyal non-discretionary base

failure_modes: applying the leakage uniformly to emergency-dispatch and relationship-driven services that do not cross-shop
treating the leakage as measured when it is a behavioral estimate
acceptance_tests: the analysis states Modesto's size and distance and ranks sub-categories by exposure to leakage, flagging the figure as a behavioral estimate
revisit_triggers: a major supply house or trade firm opens in Modesto or Turlock
a cross-shop leakage study is produced
a big-box installed-services program expands or contracts

base.update_signal: regional trade supply in Modesto or Turlock shifts

nodes.definition: Lay down the published, cited cost-structure backbone every sub-category model is read against: plumbing/electrical service-and-repair gross 35-55%, labor ~25-35%, net 10-20%; HVAC gross 20-35% install / higher on repair, high equipment COGS, net 5-12%; flooring gross 25-40%, high special-order material COGS, net 5-12%; landscape maintenance gross 45-55%, labor-dominant 40-50%, net 10-20%; landscape install gross 35-50%, 20-30% material, net 10-15%; janitorial gross 40-55%, labor 50-60% (labor IS the product), net 10-25%. Labor burden adds ~25-40% on top of base wages (FICA, FUTA/SUTA, workers' comp, benefits), and emergency/after-hours repair is the highest-margin work. These are planning benchmarks from ServiceTitan/Projul/Level/Aspire/Jobber 2026, not audited operator P&Ls, and they are the lens that turns a revenue band into a margin reality.

the labor-burden uplift
the emergency-repair-highest-margin fact
the planning-prior status of the figures

pros.claim: Pairing every revenue band with the gross/labor/material/net benchmark stops high gross from being mistaken for high profit
pros.example: an established multi-truck plumber benchmarking $2M+ gross still nets only 10-20%, which the backbone makes explicit

cons.example: a coastal-CA labor benchmark overstates cost for a Turlock crew at lower-middle valley wages

reading a benchmark range as a single point estimate

nodes.definition: Define the only honest way to attach a revenue band to a sub-category when no per-business revenue is public: take a published productivity benchmark (plumbing $350k-$550k/truck, HVAC $400k-$650k/truck, electrical $180k-$250k rev/electrician, flooring ~$563k gross/installer-firm, landscape ~$107k rev/employee, janitorial $75k-$200k small / $250k-$1M+ multi-contract) and scale it by an observable Turlock size signal (years in business, residential-vs-commercial language, showroom presence, 24/7 dispatch, fleet/crew language), then tag the result 'estimate, not actual', assign a confidence level, and name the confirmation path (CSLB license status, CDTFA sales-tax receipts, or fleet/crew headcount). Unit counts (trucks/crews/electricians per firm) are themselves unknown, so bands are wide on purpose; Central Valley wage/ticket levels sit below coastal CA, so true local figures cluster at the lower-middle of each band.

included: benchmark-per-truck/tech/employee-times-size-signal method
the estimate-not-actual label, confidence and confirmation path
the unknown-unit-count caveat and lower-middle-band correction

pros.claim: A labeled benchmark band gives a defensible planning number without ever claiming a private business's actual revenue
pros.example: a solo owner-operator plumber at $350k-$550k/truck scales to a band tagged estimate with a CSLB-status confirmation path

cons.claim: A benchmark band can be over-trusted if the size signal is mis-observed or the confidence label is dropped
cons.example: treating a years-in-business signal as a precise truck count when the fleet size is unknown

failure_modes: dropping the estimate-not-actual label and presenting a band as a fact
reading a wide band as a point estimate without the unknown-unit-count caveat
acceptance_tests: every revenue band produced carries the estimate-not-actual label, a confidence level, the size signal used, and a named confirmation source, and the unknown-unit-count and lower-middle-band caveats are stated

nodes.definition: Explain the four labor archetypes the sector resolves into and where each breaks. Licensed-pro gated trades (electrical, HVAC, plumbing) are legally bound to a CSLB license holder / RMO with journeyman/apprentice crews working under that license, where skilled labor is a hard supply constraint not just a cost line (AEI #885461, Frayer #1101008, Saunders 1948, Johnson 1960). Recurring-contract route crews (janitorial, landscape maintenance) sell crew-hours on standing accounts — the most predictable revenue, thinnest COGS, most labor-percentage-sensitive (50-60% janitorial, 40-50% landscape). Project/install crews (flooring, landscape install, water-heater/panel/system swaps) run material-plus-labor jobs at higher COGS. Mobile dispatch + 24/7 emergency (plumbing/HVAC) carries the highest margins. The dominant model is licensed owner-operator + W-2 field crew(s) of roughly 2-12 staff; there is no booth/chair-rental model here.

included: the four labor archetypes and their predictability/COGS/labor-share profiles
skilled labor as a hard supply constraint
the 2-12 owner-operator-plus-crew staffing read

pros.claim: Naming the four archetypes explains why predictability, COGS and labor-share differ sharply across the sector
pros.example: a janitorial route crew on standing accounts is the most predictable revenue with the thinnest COGS but the highest labor share

cons.claim: The license-tied archetype makes labor a supply constraint that no cost model captures, so a benchmark labor line understates the real bottleneck
cons.example: a plumber unable to grow because journeyman supply, not demand, caps the crew

failure_modes: modeling a gated trade at benchmark labor cost and missing that skilled-labor scarcity is the real constraint
assuming a recurring-route crew model scales like a project-install one
acceptance_tests: the four archetypes are named with their predictability/COGS/labor-share, skilled-labor scarcity is flagged as a hard supply constraint, and the owner-operator-plus-crew staffing range is stated
revisit_triggers: a journeyman/tech labor shortage or wage change
a firm shifts between recurring-route and project-install work
a minimum-wage change alters the hired-labor alternative

base.update_signal: a labor archetype mix, skilled-labor supply, or wage-floor change occurs

nodes.definition: Map the seasonality that shapes each sub-category's cash flow and crew planning: HVAC is strongly seasonal with a summer 100F+ cooling peak that drives an emergency surge (and a secondary winter heating spike); landscaping runs spring-fall install-and-mow with winter cleanup and dormant pruning; plumbing and electrical are less seasonal, tied to housing-stock age, remodels and emergencies; janitorial is non-seasonal recurring nights and weekends, the steadiest revenue in the set; flooring tracks the remodel and real-estate cycle and softens when rates rise. The mechanical trades convert weather amplification into emergency-premium margin, while the recurring services trade seasonality for steadiness, so a pro forma must model each sub-category's peak-and-trough rather than a flat annual band.

weather amplification of HVAC and the emergency premium
the non-seasonal steadiness of janitorial and the rate-sensitivity of flooring

pros.example: an HVAC firm staffing for the July 100F+ surge and carrying a softer shoulder season

failure_modes: modeling a seasonal trade on a flat annual band and missing the trough cash crunch
ignoring that flooring and discretionary install demand soften when interest rates tighten

nodes.definition: Establish the licensing gate that governs every licensed trade. A CSLB license is required for any project where labor plus materials is $500 or more (the threshold above which covered work cannot be legally bid), tied to a Responsible Managing Officer. The relevant Class-C classifications are C-10 Electrical (AEI, Frayer), C-20 HVAC (Horizon, Saunders, and the HVAC side of DeHart/Turlock Plumbing H&A), C-36 Plumbing (Johnson, Mainline, PRO, Turlock Plumbing Co, DeHart), C-27 Landscaping (the seven landscapers, with Capote's concrete possibly invoking C-8), and C-15 Flooring (Arrow, Turlock Floor Covering). Janitorial is generally NOT CSLB-gated — it runs on a city business license plus a liability/janitorial bond instead. This classification gate, plus skilled-labor scarcity, is what sorts the thin licensed trades from the crowded barely-gated tail.

included: the CSLB license requirement and the $500/$1,000 labor-plus-materials threshold
the C-10/C-20/C-36/C-27/C-15 classifications mapped to firms
the janitorial not-CSLB-gated exception

pros.claim: Treating the CSLB classification as the binding entry gate explains why the licensed trades stay thin and concentrated
pros.example: a new electrical entrant must hold a C-10 and an RMO before bidding any covered panel job

cons.claim: The license is necessary but not sufficient, since skilled-labor scarcity gates entry even for a license holder
cons.example: a licensed firm unable to staff a crew despite holding the classification

failure_modes: assuming a city business license clears covered trade work that actually requires a Class-C license
treating the janitorial exemption as applying to the licensed trades
acceptance_tests: the CSLB requirement, the labor-plus-materials threshold and the C-10/C-20/C-36/C-27/C-15 classifications are stated with sources and the janitorial exception is named
revisit_triggers: a CSLB classification or threshold rule changes
a firm adds or drops a licensed trade line
a janitorial-bond or city-license requirement changes

base.update_signal: a CSLB classification, threshold, or janitorial-exemption rule changes

nodes.definition: Define the financial-compliance gate layered on the CSLB classification: a $25,000 contractor bond on file for all licensees (LLCs carry an additional $100,000 worker bond), general-liability premium, and workers' compensation required for any contractor with employees — with C-20 HVAC unable to claim a WC exemption regardless of employee status. Fixed annual gates include the bond premium, GL premium, WC (rate-driven, higher for HVAC-class risk) and CSLB renewal (~$450/cycle range). The binding near-term item is the SB 216 push toward workers-comp-for-all-licensees, deferred from 1/1/2026 to 1/1/2028 by SB 1455 — a cost-shock that will raise the fixed-cost floor on the smallest licensed operators when it lands, tightening the licensed-trade count further. EPA Section 608 refrigerant certification and the A2L transition add a parallel HVAC-specific gate.

included: the $25,000 bond and $100,000 LLC worker bond
GL and workers-comp with the C-20 no-exemption rule
the SB 216/SB 1455 deferral to 2028
EPA 608/A2L refrigerant certification

pros.claim: Stating the bond, WC and SB 1455 timing shows the real fixed-cost floor under a licensed trade beyond the license itself
pros.example: a small C-20 HVAC operator unable to dodge WC and facing the 2028 cost-shock

cons.claim: The future SB 1455 cost-shock is a timing item whose magnitude per operator is not yet priced, so it is a moving part not a fixed number
cons.example: the WC-for-all-licensees cost varying by class and headcount when it lands in 2028

failure_modes: budgeting the license but omitting the bond, GL, WC and renewal fixed annual floor
missing the EPA 608/A2L gate that sits beside the financial-compliance one for HVAC
acceptance_tests: the $25,000 bond, the WC requirement with the C-20 no-exemption rule, the SB 216/SB 1455 2028 deferral and the EPA 608 certification are stated with sources as the financial-compliance floor
revisit_triggers: a bond, GL or WC rate or rule changes
the SB 1455 WC-for-all-licensees deadline approaches or moves
an EPA refrigerant-transition rule changes equipment cost

nodes.definition: Map the capital-equipment intensity that gates entry independent of demand: electrical is medium (vans, hand/power tools, testers, conduit bender, minimal shop); HVAC is medium-high (vans, recovery machines, gauges, vacuum pumps, EPA-spec tooling); plumbing is medium (vans, drain machines/cameras, press tools, jetters); flooring is low-medium plus the one true storefront buildout (showroom plus install tools — saws, stretchers); landscaping is low-medium (trucks/trailers, mowers, skid steer, hand tools); janitorial is low (vacuums, buffers/auto-scrubbers, vehicles, no storefront). The defining sector capital is trucks, tools and licenses on a no-rent mobile profile, with flooring the lone showroom exception. nodes.definition: Model the HVAC sub-category (2 primary: Horizon 20+ yr, Saunders since 1948; plus ~2 functional via plumbing cross-sellers DeHart and Turlock Plumbing H&A). The cost center is high-COGS equipment (condensers, furnaces, coils, refrigerant, ducting from Ferguson HVAC/Watsco/Johnstone), giving the thinnest install gross (20-35%, higher on repair) and net 5-12%. It is the most weather-amplified trade — the summer 100F+ valley peak drives an emergency surge — and carries a C-20 license that cannot claim a WC exemption plus EPA 608/A2L refrigerant exposure and medium-high capex (recovery machines, vacuum pumps). It benchmarks $1M-$3M for established multi-truck firms and $400k-$700k for smaller ones, estimate-not-actual. Multi-generation longevity (Saunders 1948) and replacement-heavy demand sustain it despite the thin install net, and functional capacity (~4) exceeds the headline count of 2.

nodes.definition: Model the electrical sub-category (2 firms: Applied Electrical Services / AEI #885461, Frayer Electric #1101008), the thinnest licensed trade and the clearest white space on count. It runs service-and-repair plus light-commercial economics — gross 35-55%, labor ~25-35%, net 10-20% — on a C-10 license and medium capex (vans, testers, bender), with inputs from Graybar/Rexel/CED and gear from Square D/Eaton/Siemens. A journeyman targets $180k-$250k revenue/electrician at 4.5-5x burdened cost on service; 1-3 electricians benchmark $300k-$600k and a small commercial-capable firm $600k-$1.5M, estimate-not-actual. Only two cataloged C-10 firms serve a 73k city with rising solar/EV-charger/panel-upgrade demand, so local independent electrical capacity looks under-supplied — a thin count plus rising non-discretionary demand is genuine white space, because the licensing-and-skilled-labor moat that suppresses entry also protects whoever clears it.

nodes.definition: Model the flooring sub-category (2 firms: Arrow Floor Covering, Turlock Floor Covering), the lone storefront/showroom model in the sector. It pairs a showroom sampling manufacturer goods (Shaw, Mohawk, Mannington) with dispatched install crews, running gross 25-40%, install labor ~15-25%, high special-order material COGS, and a thin net 5-12% on a C-15 license. Material is largely special-order cut-to-job (~1-3 weeks), not deep warehoused stock, and the showroom adds ~$60k fixed lease that the rest of the no-rent mobile sector avoids. It benchmarks $500k-$1.5M for showroom-plus-install, estimate-not-actual. The sub-category is thin because big-box installed flooring (Home Depot/Lowe's) and Modesto retailers absorb much demand, and it tracks the remodel/real-estate cycle, softening when interest rates and remodel budgets tighten.

nodes.definition: Model landscape maintenance, the labor-dominant half of the most-crowded sub-category (within the 7 landscapers: Lopez 30+ yr, Visionary tree care, JNG, Turlock Landscaping, plus the maintenance arms of others). The product sold is recurring crew-hours on standing accounts (offices, ag facilities, HOAs, residences), giving gross 45-55% but labor-dominant 40-50% and very low material COGS (2-6%), net 10-20%. Entry is near-trivial (truck-and-mower capex, C-27 light gate, large Hispanic labor/entrepreneur base) and the supply houses (SiteOne, Ewing) are shared, so commodity maintenance is a race to the bottom competed on price and relationships. The operational risk is labor cost/availability, not material supply; defensibility comes only from contract retention, and the format overlaps heavily with the uncataloged informal tail.

near-trivial entry and the race-to-the-bottom price floor
contract retention as the only moat and the informal-tail overlap

nodes.definition: Model landscape install/design/hardscape, the differentiated half above the commodity-mowing floor (Capote with a concrete cross-sell possibly invoking C-8, Valley Nursery 20 yr, Diaz & Flores minimal-chemical whole-systems, Turlock Landscaping design/irrigation/lighting). It runs material-plus-labor project economics — gross 35-50%, ~15-25% labor, 20-30% material — net 10-15% on a C-27 (plus possible C-8 concrete), with inputs from SiteOne/Ewing/Horizon (Hunter/Rain Bird/Toro) and rock/aggregate/concrete yards. nodes.definition: Model the janitorial/cleaning sub-category (3 cataloged plus a deep informal tail: ASAP 30+ yr commercial, Ultimate commercial/residential, Barbara's residential/move-out 15 yr). The product sold is recurring crew-hours on standing accounts, where labor IS the product at 50-60% of revenue with very low chemical/paper COGS (WAXIE, Imperial Dade), gross 40-55% commercial, net 10-25%. It is generally NOT CSLB-gated — running on a city business license plus a liability/janitorial bond — with low capex (vacuums, auto-scrubbers, vehicles, no storefront), so entry is trivial and the informal residential market is deep. Competition splits between commercial-contract players (ASAP, Ultimate — stickier, higher revenue, $250k-$900k) and residential/move-out operators (Barbara's — lower revenue, higher churn, $75k-$200k), both estimate-not-actual. The moat is contract retention, not supply or capex.

nodes.definition: Model the mobile-dispatch and 24/7 emergency premium that overlays the mechanical trades (PRO Plumbers and Turlock Plumbing Co advertise 24/7 across Stanislaus County; HVAC carries an analogous summer-emergency premium). After-hours, non-discretionary repair at the moment of failure — a dead water heater, a failed AC in a 100F July, a tripping panel — carries low price sensitivity and the sector's highest margins (repair gross 35-55% materially exceeds install gross). The model requires standby dispatch capacity, on-call crew labor and rapid supply-house access, trading higher labor-availability cost for premium tickets. It is a margin lever layered on plumbing, HVAC and electrical rather than a standalone format, and it is a key part of why those licensed trades are defensible against commodity competition and big-box leakage.

the standby-dispatch and on-call-labor cost

nodes.definition: Synthesize the per-sub-category saturation read that explains why ~22 cataloged firms is the visible floor and where headroom remains. Catalog density is 3.0/10k (22/73k x 10,000), a floor not a ceiling; adjusted true density with the informal tail is plausibly 5-8/10k. Crowded/at-floor easy-entry (do not add): landscape maintenance (most crowded, race-to-the-bottom), residential/move-out cleaning. Moderately served/defensible: plumbing (6, licensing + 24/7 brand), HVAC (2 primary, ~4 functional, replacement-driven), flooring (2, big-box/Modesto-capped). Headroom/white space, ranked: independent electrical (thinnest licensed trade vs rising solar/EV/panel demand — best-supported), commercial HVAC for the ag/food-facility belt, premium/water-wise landscape design, and a succession-acquisition path into multi-generation incumbents (Saunders 1948, Johnson 1960, Lopez 30+ yr, ASAP 30+ yr). The count is held down by the demand ceiling and Modesto leakage; its internal shape is set by the licensing/skilled-labor barrier.

nodes.definition: Model the succession-acquisition entry path the green-field saturation read alone misses. The sector skews heavily to long-tenured owner-operated incumbents — Saunders (1948), Johnson (1960), Lopez (30+ yr), ASAP (30+ yr), Mainline (28+ yr), Valley Nursery (20 yr) — whose owner age implies real succession and continuity risk and therefore an acquisition opportunity rather than a build. For a buyer, acquiring an established license-tied book of business sidesteps the two barriers that otherwise gate the licensed trades: the CSLB license/RMO continuity and the brand-tenure and skilled-crew base that take years to build. The path is strongest in the gated trades (plumbing, HVAC, electrical) where the moat is hardest to build new, and it converts a thin-count no-build verdict into a defensible buy verdict, conditioned on RMO/license transfer and crew retention.

nodes.definition: Compose the merged go/no-go verdict on entering or running a given sub-category, the synthesis the whole KB builds toward. It intersects three lenses: demand headroom (SATURATION_WHITESPACE), the licensing/labor/capex gate (CSLB_LICENSE_GATE, BOND_INSURANCE_WC_GATE, FLEET_TOOL_CAPEX), and the margin reality (COST_STRUCTURE_BENCHMARKS, LABOR_MODEL_ARCHETYPES), and it folds in the SUCCESSION_ACQUISITION_PATH as the buy-not-build alternative. The reconciled rule: do not add a ninth commodity-mowing landscaper or a fourth residential cleaner into the price-competitive easy-entry tail; the defensible headroom is independent electrical (above all), commercial HVAC for the ag/food-facility belt, premium water-wise landscape design, and a succession-acquisition path into license-tied incumbent books — each viable only after clearing the CSLB classification and the binding skilled-labor constraint (and, for HVAC, the WC-no-exemption and EPA-608 gates). A white space that is demand-true but labor- or license-gated is a no-go until the gate is cleared.

conflict_axes.name: licensed_moat_vs_modesto_leakage
conflict_axes.description: The licensing/skilled-labor moat protects some thin trades while Modesto leakage also thins the count; a count read can over-weight either force.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: apply the moat view to non-discretionary emergency-dispatch trades and the leakage view to high-ticket cross-shopped flooring and specialty work

conflict_axes.name: demand_headroom_vs_license_labor_gate
conflict_axes.description: A sub-category with real demand headroom may still be gated by CSLB licensing, the bond/WC floor, skilled-labor scarcity or capex, so demand-true is not the same as enterable.
poles: enter only where the license/labor gate clears
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: treat a demand-true but license- or labor-gated white space as a no-go until the binding gate is cleared

conflict_axes.name: skilled_labor_scarcity_vs_demand
conflict_axes.description: Rising non-discretionary demand argues for entering a thin licensed trade while journeyman/tech scarcity caps how fast that entry can be staffed.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: treat skilled labor as a hard supply constraint, not just a cost line, and confirm crew availability before acting on demand

conflict_axes.name: easy_entry_survival_vs_no_moat
conflict_axes.description: Near-zero entry lets a landscaper or cleaner start cheaply, but the same easy entry and shared supply leave no moat beyond contract retention, so survival is a price-and-retention grind.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: enter Engine-B services only on a sticky contract base, not on low capex alone, and model the race-to-the-bottom price floor

conflict_axes.name: emergency_premium_vs_standby_cost
conflict_axes.description: The 24/7 emergency premium is the highest-margin work but requires standby dispatch and on-call labor that raise the labor-availability cost the benchmark hides.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: price the standby and on-call crew cost into the premium and confirm the surge volume justifies 24/7 capacity

conflict_axes.name: wc_for_all_costshock_vs_small_operator
conflict_axes.description: The SB 216/SB 1455 workers-comp-for-all-licensees push (deferred to 2028) raises the fixed-cost floor on the smallest licensed operators, trading compliance against the survival of sub-scale firms.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: model the 2028 WC-for-all cost-shock into the smallest licensed operator's fixed floor before assuming it survives

conflict_axes.name: showroom_storefront_vs_no_rent_mobile
conflict_axes.description: The flooring showroom wins special-order install work but carries a fixed lease the no-rent mobile trades avoid, a storefront-margin-vs-fixed-cost trade unique in the sector.
poles: run the showroom for install conversion
stay mobile to avoid the lease
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: justify the showroom only where special-order install conversion services the fixed lease against big-box leakage

conflict_axes.name: catalog_floor_vs_true_density
conflict_axes.description: The 3.0/10k cataloged density reads as thin while the informal cash-basis tail pushes true operating density to 5-8/10k, so a 'thin' sub-category may be thin only among cataloged firms.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: treat every catalog count as a floor and read 'thin' as thin-among-cataloged-firms, especially for landscaping and cleaning

edge_cases.description: An HVAC install pro forma reads the high gross revenue band as profit and ignores the 5-12% install net
edge_cases.trigger: a high equipment-COGS install band is mistaken for a high-margin one
edge_cases.mitigation: pair the HVAC gross band with the thin install net and lead margin reads with emergency repair, not install

edge_cases.description: An electrical entrant acts on the thin count and rising demand but cannot staff journeymen
edge_cases.trigger: a white-space call ignores the skilled-labor supply cap
edge_cases.mitigation: confirm journeyman/apprentice crew availability before treating thin-count electrical as enterable

edge_cases.description: A licensed trade is budgeted on the license but not the bond, GL, WC and renewal fixed floor
edge_cases.trigger: an entry plan omits the financial-compliance gate beyond the CSLB classification
edge_cases.mitigation: budget the $25,000 bond, GL, WC and renewal floor and price the 2028 WC-for-all cost-shock

edge_cases.description: A C-20 HVAC operator assumes a workers-comp exemption that does not exist
edge_cases.trigger: a small HVAC firm tries to dodge WC regardless of employee status
edge_cases.mitigation: carry workers-comp for C-20 unconditionally and model the SB 1455 2028 cost-shock

edge_cases.description: A truck-and-mower landscaper is added into the saturated commodity-maintenance count
edge_cases.trigger: an entry rests on low capex and a deep labor base, ignoring the race-to-the-bottom floor
edge_cases.mitigation: enter landscape only on a differentiated install/design/eco base or a sticky contract book, not commodity mowing

edge_cases.description: A flooring pro forma uses the no-rent mobile profile and omits the showroom fixed lease
edge_cases.trigger: the lone storefront model is costed like the rest of the mobile sector
edge_cases.mitigation: include the ~$60k showroom fixed lease and confirm special-order install conversion services it

edge_cases.description: A '24/7 emergency' line is advertised without the standby crew and supply access to deliver it
edge_cases.trigger: the dispatch premium is claimed without the on-call labor and supply-house capacity behind it
edge_cases.mitigation: staff and price the standby/on-call crew and rapid supply access before promising 24/7 response

edge_cases.description: The 3.0/10k catalog density is read as a true total, ignoring the informal tail
edge_cases.trigger: someone treats the catalog floor as a ceiling and calls a sub-category saturated
edge_cases.mitigation: label the 3.0/10k a floor and adjust toward the 5-8/10k informal-tail estimate before a saturation call

edge_cases.description: A named business's revenue is requested or asserted as an actual figure
edge_cases.trigger: a question demands the real sales of a specific Turlock trade firm
edge_cases.mitigation: refuse to state actual revenue; provide only a labeled benchmark estimate with confidence and a CSLB/sales-tax confirmation path

edge_cases.description: A supplier-to-named-business link is upgraded from inference to a stated account
edge_cases.trigger: an answer asserts a specific firm buys from a named supply house without a source
edge_cases.mitigation: keep supplier links labeled representative inference unless a cited source states the account

edge_cases.description: A demand-true white space is treated as enterable while a license or labor gate blocks it
edge_cases.trigger: a headroom call ignores CSLB licensing, the bond/WC floor or skilled-labor scarcity
edge_cases.mitigation: run every white space through the license/labor/capex gate before issuing a go verdict

workflow.action: Size the homeowner, commercial and property-manager demand floor
workflow.description: State the population, household, income and demand-source figures as cited facts or labeled estimates and split discretionary vs non-discretionary
workflow.gate: population, household count, income and the discretionary split are stated with range and confidence

workflow.action: Partition the sector into its two engines
workflow.description: Assign each sub-category to the licensed-event-driven or easy-entry-recurring engine with its moat profile
workflow.gate: each engine is defined with its moats and mapped to its sub-categories

workflow.description: Identify which job types and channels leak to Modesto and which sub-categories are exposed
workflow.gate: Modesto size/distance stated and sub-categories ranked by leakage exposure

workflow.description: State gross/labor/material/net benchmarks by sub-category with sources and the labor-burden uplift
workflow.gate: gross, labor, material and net ranges are stated as cited planning priors

workflow.description: Define benchmark-per-truck/tech/employee-times-size-signal banding with the estimate label and confirmation path
workflow.gate: every band carries the estimate-not-actual label, a confidence, a size signal and a confirmation source

workflow.action: Identify the labor archetypes and supply map
workflow.description: Name the four labor archetypes and the shared supply houses per sub-category as inference
workflow.gate: the four archetypes and skilled-labor scarcity are stated and supply nodes are labeled inference

workflow.action: Establish the licensing, bond and capex gates
workflow.description: State the CSLB classification, the bond/WC floor and the fleet/tool capex intensity per sub-category
workflow.gate: the CSLB classifications, the $25,000 bond/WC floor and the capex intensity are stated with sources

workflow.action: Model each licensed mechanical trade's unit economics
workflow.description: For plumbing, HVAC and electrical state cost center, license, benchmark band and the emergency/white-space tie
workflow.gate: each mechanical trade names its cost center, labeled band and the gate or lever that decides viability

workflow.action: Model the flooring, landscape and janitorial formats
workflow.description: State the showroom-install, recurring-route and project-install models with their margin and entry profiles
workflow.gate: each format names its product, labeled band and moat (or lack of one)

workflow.description: Tie the after-hours non-discretionary repair premium to the standby/on-call cost across the mechanical trades
workflow.gate: the after-hours premium and the standby/on-call cost are stated

workflow.action: Synthesize saturation, white space and the merged go/no-go
workflow.description: Give the at-floor/defensible/headroom read, rank the white space, then intersect demand, gate and margin into an add/avoid verdict
workflow.gate: each sub-category has a saturation read, the white space is ranked, and the verdict is conditioned on clearing the CSLB and skilled-labor gate

dominance_rules.rule: The honesty label dominates any revenue claim
dominance_rules.rationale: no per-business revenue is public, so a band may never be presented as an actual figure
dominance_rules.trigger: any dollar figure is attached to a named business or sub-category
dominance_rules.action: tag it estimate-not-actual with a confidence and confirmation path, and refuse an actual-revenue claim

dominance_rules.rule: The license-and-labor gate dominates demand headroom in any entry verdict
dominance_rules.rationale: a demand-true white space that cannot clear CSLB licensing or staff skilled labor is not enterable
dominance_rules.trigger: a go recommendation rests on demand alone
dominance_rules.action: withhold the go until the binding license/labor gate is shown clearable

dominance_rules.rule: Net margin dominates gross revenue in judging attractiveness
dominance_rules.rationale: high-gross trades still net only single-to-low-double digits and install is thinner than repair
dominance_rules.trigger: a sub-category is judged by its revenue band alone
dominance_rules.action: pair the band with its gross/labor/material/net benchmark before deciding

dominance_rules.rule: Skilled-labor scarcity dominates the licensed-trade entry decision
dominance_rules.rationale: journeyman/tech supply, not demand, is the binding constraint on the gated trades
dominance_rules.trigger: a licensed-trade entry is scoped on rising demand without confirming crew supply
dominance_rules.action: confirm journeyman/apprentice availability before treating the trade as enterable

dominance_rules.rule: The workers-comp requirement dominates the small-HVAC-operator cost model
dominance_rules.rationale: C-20 cannot claim a WC exemption and the 2028 WC-for-all push raises the fixed floor
dominance_rules.trigger: an HVAC cost model omits unconditional WC or the SB 1455 cost-shock
dominance_rules.action: carry WC for C-20 and model the 2028 fixed-cost floor

dominance_rules.rule: Saturation dominates demand depth for at-floor easy-entry formats
dominance_rules.rationale: a deep labor base does not justify adding to a race-to-the-bottom, no-moat count
dominance_rules.trigger: an addition is proposed for commodity landscape maintenance or residential cleaning
dominance_rules.action: default to no-add and pursue differentiation or a sticky contract base instead

dominance_rules.rule: The catalog floor dominates any saturation total
dominance_rules.rationale: the 3.0/10k count is a floor that the informal cash-basis tail pushes to 5-8/10k
dominance_rules.trigger: a catalog count is read as a true total
dominance_rules.action: label it a floor and adjust toward the 5-8/10k informal-tail estimate before a saturation call

dominance_rules.rule: The emergency-repair premium dominates the install margin read
dominance_rules.rationale: after-hours repair carries the sector's highest margin while install is the thinnest
dominance_rules.trigger: a mechanical-trade margin is read off install gross
dominance_rules.action: lead the margin read with emergency repair and treat install as the thin line

dominance_rules.rule: Documented links dominate inferred supplier links
dominance_rules.rationale: supplier-to-business accounts are representative inference unless a cited source states them
dominance_rules.action: label it inference unless a cited source confirms the account

anti_rework_rules.rule: Attach the estimate-not-actual label when the band is first produced, not after review
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a revenue figure circulating as a fact and having to be retracted

anti_rework_rules.rule: Confirm skilled-labor crew availability before scoping a licensed-trade entry
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a thin-count electrical or HVAC plan stalling on an unstaffable journeyman gate

anti_rework_rules.rule: Budget the bond, GL, WC and renewal floor in the same step as the license
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a licensed-trade plan reopened when the financial-compliance floor surfaces

anti_rework_rules.rule: Carry unconditional workers-comp for C-20 HVAC from the outset
anti_rework_rules.prevents: an HVAC cost model redone after the no-WC-exemption rule and SB 1455 cost-shock land

anti_rework_rules.rule: Pair every revenue band with its net benchmark in the same step
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a high-gross trade being approved before the thin net is seen

anti_rework_rules.rule: Run a white space through the license/labor/capex gate before calling it an opportunity
anti_rework_rules.prevents: recommending a demand-true but license- or labor-gated sub-category and reversing the call

anti_rework_rules.rule: Include the showroom fixed lease when costing the flooring model
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a flooring plan failing on the storefront fixed cost the no-rent profile hid

anti_rework_rules.rule: Treat every catalog count as a floor, not a total, from the outset
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a saturation call anchored on the 3.0/10k floor that the informal tail invalidates

anti_rework_rules.rule: Keep supplier-to-business links labeled inference from the outset
anti_rework_rules.prevents: an inferred supply account hardening into an asserted one that must later be corrected

iteration_protocol.trigger: CSLB license-status or CDTFA sales-tax data becomes available for a firm
iteration_protocol.action: replace the labeled revenue bands and size signals with confirmed figures and re-rank confidence

iteration_protocol.trigger: a firm opens or closes, changing a per-sub-category count
iteration_protocol.action: update the saturation read and the merged go/no-go for that sub-category

iteration_protocol.trigger: the SB 216/SB 1455 workers-comp-for-all-licensees deadline approaches or moves
iteration_protocol.action: re-price the licensed-operator fixed-cost floor and the HVAC and entry verdicts

iteration_protocol.trigger: a Census ACS refresh changes population, income or demographics
iteration_protocol.action: re-size the demand floor and re-map the two-engine and saturation reads

iteration_protocol.trigger: an equipment, refrigerant or material price swing (condensers, A2L refrigerant, water heaters, aggregate)
iteration_protocol.action: update the affected sub-category cost centers and the supply and cost-structure nodes

iteration_protocol.trigger: a journeyman/tech skilled-labor supply or wage change
iteration_protocol.action: re-evaluate the labor archetypes and the licensed-trade entry verdicts

iteration_protocol.trigger: a cross-shop leakage study or measured Modesto-capture figure is produced
iteration_protocol.action: replace the behavioral leakage estimate and re-rank the at-floor and headroom reads

iteration_protocol.trigger: a solar/EV/panel-upgrade demand shift or a new C-10 entrant
iteration_protocol.action: re-evaluate the electrical white-space read and the merged go/no-go

priority_rationale: The demand floor, two-engine split and Modesto leakage come first because every sub-category judgment depends on knowing the size and shape of demand and where defensibility lives; the cost-structure backbone, labeled-revenue method, labor archetypes, supply map and seasonality next, because they are the lenses that turn demand into unit economics; the CSLB licensing, bond/WC and fleet/tool-capex gates next, because they decide enterability independent of demand; the eight sub-category and emergency-dispatch models then apply all of that to the concrete Turlock firms; and the saturation synthesis and merged go/no-go come last because they compose every upstream output into a defensible add/avoid verdict.
